chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place on a school playground and its fair. Children turn on the spot, a giant wheel comes back to its starting seat, a straw and a paper fan turn, and a minute hand goes round. Turning shows what an angle is, how to name it and how to measure it as a part of a turn. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, turns, measures and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Seven tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every Let Us Do part, Let Us Think question, Fun with Turns question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: An angle is a turn
points.text: Every angle is shown as a start mark, a turning arm and the part of a full turn it has made. Angles are measured as parts of a full turn: halves, quarters, eighths, sixths and twelfths.

points.title: Only the book's numbers
points.text: The pieces, the clock positions, the compass and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.

modules.module_summary: Full turns and half turns in games, clocks and wheels, halves and quarters that make a full turn, how far everyday things turn, and the right, acute, obtuse and straight angles that a turn makes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: four children are playing Statue. They keep turning around, and when Statue is called they freeze. Will all four be facing the same way?
2. Four children, A, B, C and D, stand in a row on the playground. They are playing Statue.
3. They keep turning around. Then someone calls Statue, and every child freezes where they are.
4. Look at the four children now. They are not all facing the same way. Some turned a lot and some turned a little, but every one of them turned.
5. Can you tell which child has made a full turn and which has made a half turn?
6. Where do you see turns in real life? Think of one example, then try the Statue Turn tool on the next screen.

tool_config.title: Statue Turn
tool_config.idea: Find out by turning a child on the spot that a full turn brings the child back to the starting position and a half turn leaves the child facing the opposite way. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the two turns. Only full turns and half turns appear in this tool: no angle names and no fractions of a turn.
tool_config.screen: The school playground at morning break, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A ring is painted on the ground in the middle, and on it stands a child with one foot fixed on a mark, shown large from a high viewpoint. A teal start arrow is painted on the ground and shows the way the child faced at the start; it never moves. An orange turning arrow follows the child's face. The child's free foot leaves a trace line on the ring, so a full turn draws a complete circle and a half turn draws a half-moon, as with Ashutosh and Sahana in your maths book. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: a big Turn button (press and hold to turn the child slowly, or drag the child round); a big STATUE! button that freezes the child; a check row under the child with three buttons, Same way as the start, Opposite way and Neither; three bins, Full turn, Half turn and Neither, for four statue picture cards; a row of explanation cards that click into an answer strip; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the child to the start for this card), Reset (restores the whole tool), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a facing label, Facing now: the same way as the start, the opposite way, or neither; a turn label that says Full turn or Half turn only when the child faces the start way or the opposite way; and a card number out of 6.
student_does: Look at the four children of the story who keep turning around and freeze when Statue is called. Here is one child on a ring with the start arrow on the ground. Press and hold Turn, then press STATUE! to freeze, and look at where the child faces compared with the start arrow.

Turn Ashutosh until he faces the same way as at the start, turn Sahana until she faces the opposite way, freeze a child who faces neither the start way nor the opposite way, and sort four statue picture cards into Full turn, Half turn and Neither.

Answer the question from the story, Can you recognise the child in the picture who has made a full turn? Who has made a half turn? How do you know? Build your answer from the cards. Then give an example of a turn from real life.
challenges: Card 1: turn Ashutosh until he faces the same way as at the start, then press STATUE!. What has his free foot drawn, and what turn is it? Answer: a complete circle, so it is a full turn. He is back at the starting position.

Card 2: turn Sahana until she faces the opposite way from the start arrow, then press STATUE!. What has her free foot drawn, and what turn is it? Answer: a half-moon, so it is a half turn. She faces the opposite way.

Card 3 (practice values): turn a child until the child faces neither the start way nor the opposite way, and press STATUE!. Is it a full turn, a half turn or neither? Answer: neither. The child does not face the start way and does not face the opposite way.

Card 4 (practice values): sort four statue picture cards into Full turn, Half turn and Neither. Card A faces the start way, card B faces the opposite way, card C faces neither the start way nor the opposite way, card D faces the start way. Answer: A and D go to Full turn, B goes to Half turn, C goes to Neither.

Challenge: 'Can you recognise the child in the picture who has made a full turn? Who has made a half turn? How do you know? Discuss in class.' Look at the statue picture of A, B, C and D, then build your answer from the cards. Answer: A made a half turn, because A faces the opposite way. B and C made a full turn, because they face the way they faced at the start. D faces the side, so D made neither. Cards that fit: Face the same way as the start is a full turn; Face the opposite way is a half turn. Your explanation may use your own words.

Challenge: 'Give examples of real-life situations where you observe turns.' Type or pick your examples. Answer: your own examples, such as a door on its hinge, a tap, a hand of a clock or a giant wheel. Your answers may differ. Next stop: the video that names a full turn and a half turn.
feedback: While the child turns, the turning arrow follows the child's face and the foot trace draws on the ring.
On STATUE! the tool says where the child faces compared with the start arrow: Same way as the start: that is a full turn. Opposite way: that is a half turn.

Pressing STATUE! when the child faces neither the start way nor the opposite way shows a soft amber note: This child does not face the start way or the opposite way. Turn on until it does, or call it Neither.
A statue card dropped in the wrong bin slides back with a clue, for example: Where does this child face compared with the start arrow? A card in the right bin locks in with a soft chime.

An explanation card that fits clicks into the answer strip. A card that does not fit slides back with a clue such as: Does this card compare the child with the start? The tool never shows the full explanation.
tool_config.done_when: A full turn and a half turn have been made, the four cards are sorted, and the student has built an answer to the opener's question and given an example of a turn.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the start arrow on the ground. Where was the child facing at the start?
Turn the child and watch the turning arrow. Compare where the child faces now with the start arrow: the same way, the opposite way, or neither?
If the child faces the same way as at the start, it is a full turn. If the child faces the opposite way, it is a half turn.
Turn the child until the child faces the start way for a full turn, or the opposite way for a half turn, and press STATUE!. The foot trace shows a complete circle or a half-moon.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Sahana stands on one spot with one foot fixed and turns until she faces the same way as at the start. How much has she turned?
2. She has made a full turn. Her free foot drew a complete circle on the ground, and she is back at the starting position.
3. If she turns only until she faces the opposite way, her free foot draws a half-moon shape. That is a half turn.
4. The minute hand of a clock makes a full turn too. It makes a full turn when it comes back to the initial position.
5. Rule: a full turn brings you back to where you started. A half turn leaves you facing the opposite way.

content.text:
Worked example: Sahana stands on one spot facing the classroom door, with one foot fixed. (a) She turns until she faces the door again. What turn is it? (b) She starts again and turns until her back is to the door. What turn is it?
1. The start: Sahana faces the door.
2. (a): She turns and faces the door again. She is back at the starting position, so it is a full turn. Her free foot has drawn a complete circle.
3. (b): She turns until her back is to the door. She faces the opposite way, so it is a half turn. Her free foot has drawn a half-moon.
4. Check: a full turn ends where it began, and a half turn ends facing the other way.
Answer: (a): a full turn; (b): a half turn

content.text: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a seat on the giant wheel takes a half turn and then another half turn in the same direction. Where is the seat now?
2. A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E.
3. A half turn takes the seat half way round. Another half turn in the same direction takes it the rest of the way, back to E. Two half turns make a full turn.
4. A quarter turn is 1/4 of a full turn. Four quarter turns make 4/4, a full turn. Two quarter turns make 2/4, which is the same as 1/2: a half turn.
5. Rule: 2 half turns make 1 full turn, 4 quarter turns make 1 full turn, and 2 quarter turns make 1 half turn.

content.text:
Worked example: A seat on the giant wheel takes 1 half turn and then 2 quarter turns, all in the same direction. What turn is that in all?
1. A half turn is 1/2 of a full turn. Two quarter turns are 2/4, which is 1/2.
2. In all: 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/2 = 1.
3. 1 is a full turn, so the seat is back at the starting position E.
4. Check: 1 half turn is 2 quarter turns, so the seat made 2 + 2 = 4 quarter turns, and 4 quarter turns make a full turn.
Answer: A full turn, so the seat is back at E

content.question: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. What happens if Reema takes 4 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn.
steps: Four quarter turns in the same direction: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4.
4/4 = 1, so it is a full turn.
The seat is back at the starting position E.
Check: two quarter turns make a half turn, and two half turns make a full turn, so four quarter turns make a full turn.
content.answer: A full turn, because 4/4 = 1.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a door opens on its hinge. Can it turn more than a quarter turn?
2. Many everyday things turn: a tap, a door on its hinge, a clothes clip, tongs, scissors, a file cover.
3. Each one can turn only so far. The greatest turn it can make is its maximum turn.
4. To check, use a quarter turn as a guide. A quarter turn makes a square corner, like the corner of a book. Open the object as far as it goes and compare it with the corner.
5. If it opens less than the corner, it turns less than a 1/4 turn. If it opens exactly to the corner, it turns a 1/4 turn. If it opens wider than the corner, it turns more than a 1/4 turn.
6. Rule: compare the greatest turn of an object with a quarter turn: less, equal or more.

content.text:
Worked example: Three practice hinges, P, Q and R, are opened as far as they go (a practice picture). P opens exactly to the corner of a book. Q opens less than the corner. R opens wider than the corner. Compare the greatest turn of each with a quarter turn.
1. The corner of a book is a quarter turn, so it is the guide.
2. P opens exactly to the corner: its greatest turn is a 1/4 turn.
3. Q opens less than the corner: its greatest turn is less than a 1/4 turn.
4. R opens wider than the corner: its greatest turn is more than a 1/4 turn.
5. Check: all three hinges were compared with the same guide, the corner of a book.
Answer: P: a 1/4 turn; Q: less than a 1/4 turn; R: more than a 1/4 turn

tool_config.title: Quarter Turn Check
tool_config.idea: One purpose, the quarter turn as a yardstick, in two clearly separated activities. Activity 1, Halves and quarters (a short recap of the topic before): join half turns and quarter turns on the giant wheel until they make a full turn. Activity 2, Objects that turn: open everyday objects as far as they go and compare their greatest turn with a quarter turn. Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done.
tool_config.screen: The school fair at the edge of the playground, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Two big activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: The giant wheel and Activity 2: Objects that turn. Only one activity is on screen at a time, and Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done. In Activity 1 the giant wheel fills the scene: its starting seat at the top marked E, large, with a teal start mark at E, an orange curved arrow and a shaded wedge that grow as the wheel turns, and Reema standing beside it. In Activity 2 a wooden table fills the scene with the everyday objects: a clothes clip, a door with a hinge, tongs, scissors and a file cover, each with an opening arm that can be dragged, and a book corner shown as the quarter-turn guide (a square corner marker that sits on the starting arm). An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls in Activity 1: two turn buttons, Half turn and Quarter turn, that turn the wheel that much in the same direction each time they are tapped; Undo, which takes back the last turn; a row of answer cards (a half turn, a full turn). Controls in Activity 2: drag the opening arm as far as it goes (it stops at the object's own limit); a Show guide switch for the quarter-turn guide; three bins, less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn and more than a 1/4 turn, and object cards to drop into them. In both: Check, Hint, Retry (returns the wheel to E or the arm to closed), Reset (restores the activity), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: in Activity 1 the turns joined so far as a sum, for example 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, the total as a fraction of a full turn, and a note when the seat is back at E; in Activity 2 a note that compares the arm with the guide; and a card number, Activity 1 cards 1 to 3 and Activity 2 cards 1 to 4.
student_does: Activity 1: look at the giant wheel turning from E and coming back to E. Tap Half turn and watch the seat. How many half turns bring the seat back to E? Activity 2: look at the corner of a book beside an open door. Does the door open less than, exactly to or wider than the corner?

Activity 1: join a half turn and two quarter turns, then join three quarter turns and one more. Activity 2: open a practice hinge to the quarter-turn guide, open two more practice hinges, and sort them.

Activity 1: answer Reema's questions about two half turns, two quarter turns and four quarter turns. Activity 2: tick the greatest turn of the clothes clip, the door with hinge, the tongs, the scissors and the file cover.
challenges: Activity 1, card 1 (practice values): tap Half turn once and Quarter turn twice, all in the same direction. What turn is that in all? Answer: 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, a full turn, and the seat is back at E.
Activity 1, card 2 (practice values): tap Quarter turn three times, then once more. What turn is that in all? Answer: 3/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1, a full turn.

Activity 1, card 3: 'A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a ___ turn. What happens if she takes 2 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn. What happens if she takes 4 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn.' Use the wheel, then pick the answer cards. Answer: a full turn, because 1/2 + 1/2 = 1; a half turn, because 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2; a full turn, because 4/4 = 1.
Activity 2, card 1 (practice values): switch on the guide and drag the arm of practice hinge H until it meets the guide. What is its turn? Answer: a 1/4 turn.

Activity 2, card 2 (practice values): drag the arms of practice hinges K and L as far as they go. Compare each with the guide. Answer: K opens less than the guide, so less than a 1/4 turn. L opens wider than the guide, so more than a 1/4 turn.
Activity 2, card 3 (practice values): drop the three practice object cards, H, K and L, into the three bins. Answer: H goes to 1/4 turn, K to less than a 1/4 turn, L to more than a 1/4 turn.

Activity 2, card 4: 'What is the maximum possible turn in each of these cases? Check and tick.' Open the clothes clip, the door with hinge, the tongs, the scissors and the file cover as far as they go and drop each into less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn or more than a 1/4 turn. Sample answer: clothes clip, less than a 1/4 turn; door with hinge, more than a 1/4 turn; tongs, less than a 1/4 turn; scissors, a 1/4 turn; file cover, more than a 1/4 turn. Your answer may differ for your own objects.
feedback: Activity 1: each tap turns the wheel and adds to the sum, for example 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. When the total reaches 1 the wheel stops with a soft chime and the note: The seat is back at E: a full turn.
Activity 1: a wrong total shows a soft amber note, for example: Two quarter turns are 2/4, which is the same as 1/2. That is a half turn, not a full turn.

Activity 2: when an arm is dragged as far as it goes, the tool shows the wedge it made and says whether it is less than, equal to or more than the guide, for example: This hinge opens wider than the guide: more than a 1/4 turn.
Activity 2: an object card dropped in the wrong bin slides back with a clue, for example: Open it as far as it goes. Is it before, at or after the guide?
An answer card that fits clicks into place. A card that does not fit slides back with a clue. The tool never shows the full answer.

media.description: Concept video: Show how to compare the greatest turn of an everyday object with a quarter turn, as less than, equal to or more than a quarter turn. It works this example: Three practice hinges, P, Q and R, are opened as far as they go (a practice picture). P opens exactly to the corner of a book. Q opens less than the corner. R opens wider than the corner. Compare the greatest turn of each with a quarter turn.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a door opens on its hinge. Can it turn more than a quarter turn? Many everyday things turn: a tap, a door on its hinge, a clothes clip, tongs, scissors, a file cover. Each one can turn only so far. The greatest turn it can make is its maximum turn. To check, use a quarter turn as a guide. A quarter turn makes a square corner, like the corner of a book. Open the object as far as it goes and compare it with the corner. If it opens less than the corner, it turns less than a 1/4 turn. If it opens exactly to the corner, it turns a 1/4 turn. If it opens wider than the corner, it turns more than a 1/4 turn. Rule: compare the greatest turn of an object with a quarter turn: less, equal or more. 1. The corner of a book is a quarter turn, so it is the guide. 2. P opens exactly to the corner: its greatest turn is a 1/4 turn. 3. Q opens less than the corner: its greatest turn is less than a 1/4 turn. 4. R opens wider than the corner: its greatest turn is more than a 1/4 turn. 5. Check: all three hinges were compared with the same guide, the corner of a book. Answer: P: a 1/4 turn; Q: less than a 1/4 turn; R: more than a 1/4 turn

steps: A half turn is two quarter turns, so the arm and the start lie in one straight line.
A door can swing open until it is flat against the wall: a half turn.
A file cover can open until it lies flat on the table: a half turn.
A clothes clip, tongs and scissors cannot open that far.
Check: only the objects that open flat make a half turn.
content.answer: Sample answer: the door with hinge and the file cover. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Pragya holds a green straw steady and turns a yellow straw a quarter turn. What does the corner between the two straws look like?
2. Pragya joined a green and a yellow straw with a paper clip. She holds the green straw steady and turns the yellow straw around.
3. A quarter turn, 1/4 of a full turn, makes a right angle. It looks like the corner of a book.
4. Less than a quarter turn makes an acute angle. It is narrower than a right angle.
5. More than a quarter turn but less than a half turn makes an obtuse angle. It is wider than a right angle.
6. Angles arise in situations that involve a turn. A paper fan, made from folded paper and two ice cream sticks, shows the same angles when it opens.
7. Rule: a 1/4 turn is a right angle, less than a 1/4 turn is an acute angle, and more than a 1/4 turn but less than a 1/2 turn is an obtuse angle.

content.text:
Worked example: Pragya opens her paper fan to three places. At X the two end sticks make exactly a quarter turn. At Y they make a little less than a quarter turn. At Z they make more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn. Name the angle at X, at Y and at Z.
1. The guide is a quarter turn, a square corner.
2. X is exactly a quarter turn: a right angle.
3. Y is less than a quarter turn: an acute angle.
4. Z is more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn: an obtuse angle.
5. Check: X, Y and Z were all compared with the same quarter turn.
Answer: X: a right angle; Y: an acute angle; Z: an obtuse angle

content.text:
I made two quarter turns. I wonder what it is called?
It is a straight angle.
Let us look at the turns made by the paper fan, keeping one side fixed.
This shows a 1/4 turn, or a right angle.
This shows a 1/2 turn, or a straight angle.
This shows a 3/4 turn, which is more than a straight angle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Pragya turns the yellow straw a quarter turn, then another quarter turn the same way. What do the two straws look like now?
2. Two quarter turns make a half turn: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. The two straws lie in one straight line. This angle is called a straight angle.
3. A 3/4 turn is more than a half turn, so it is more than a straight angle.
4. A full turn brings the straw back to where it started.
5. The paper fan shows them all with one side fixed: a full turn, a 1/2 turn (a straight angle), a 1/4 turn (a right angle), less than a 1/4 turn (an acute angle), and between a 1/4 and a 1/2 turn (an obtuse angle).
6. Rule: a 1/2 turn is a straight angle, and a 3/4 turn is more than a straight angle.

content.text:
Worked example: Pragya's paper fan opens by a half turn and then by one more quarter turn in the same direction. What turn is that in all, and how does it compare with a straight angle?
1. A half turn is 1/2 and a quarter turn is 1/4. 1/2 is the same as 2/4.
2. In all: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.
3. A straight angle is a 1/2 turn, which is 2/4. 3/4 is more than 2/4.
4. So the turn is 3/4, more than a straight angle.
5. Check: 3 quarter turns are one quarter turn short of a full turn.
Answer: A 3/4 turn, more than a straight angle

tool_config.title: Straw and Fan Angles
tool_config.idea: Turn one arm away from a fixed arm and name the angle the turn makes: acute for less than a quarter turn, right for a quarter turn, obtuse for more than a quarter and less than a half turn, straight for a half turn, and more than a straight angle for a turn of 3/4.
tool_config.screen: Pragya's desk in the classroom corner, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. In the middle, large, a green straw lies fixed along a teal start line and a yellow straw is joined to it by a paper clip at the corner; the yellow straw turns. A shaded orange wedge between the two straws shows the turn made. Beside the straws sits a paper fan made of folded green paper with an ice cream stick at each end; one stick is fixed and the other turns, and the fan opens like the straws. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the yellow straw (or the loose fan stick) round the clip; a Show guide switch that shows three marks, the quarter turn as a square corner marker, the half turn as a straight line and the three-quarter turn; an Add a turn button that makes the next turn start where the last one stopped; a Switch to fan button; five name cards, acute angle, right angle, obtuse angle, straight angle and more than a straight angle, to tap; Check, Hint, Retry (puts the yellow straw back on the green one), Reset (restores the straws and the fan), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the turn in words, less than 1/4, 1/4, between 1/4 and 1/2, 1/2, 3/4; the name of the angle once the straw stops; and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the green and the yellow straw joined at the clip. Turn the yellow straw a quarter turn and see the square corner. What angle does the yellow straw make with the green one?
Make a right angle, an acute angle and an obtuse angle with the straw, make a straight angle with two quarter turns, and turn on to a 3/4 turn.
Use the paper fan to show different acute angles and obtuse angles, then answer whether two acute turns together can make another acute turn.
challenges: Card 1: turn the yellow straw a quarter turn from the green one and tap the name card. Answer: a right angle, a square corner.
Card 2: turn the yellow straw less than a quarter turn and tap the name card. Answer: an acute angle, narrower than a right angle.
Card 3: turn the yellow straw more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn and tap the name card. Answer: an obtuse angle, wider than a right angle.

Card 4: turn the yellow straw a quarter turn, press Add a turn, and turn it a quarter turn more. What angle do the two straws make? Answer: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, a half turn: a straight angle, the two straws lie in one straight line.
Card 5: turn the yellow straw on to a 3/4 turn and tap the name card. Answer: more than a straight angle, because 3/4 is more than 1/2.

Challenge: 'Use your paper fan to show different acute angles and obtuse angles.' Switch to the fan and open it to two acute angles and two obtuse angles; the tool names each one. Answer: any opening less than a quarter turn is acute; any opening more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn is obtuse. Your answer may differ.

Challenge: 'Make an acute turn with the straws or fan. Continue to make another acute turn. Can the two acute turns together make another acute turn?' Use Add a turn after the first turn, try two small turns and then two bigger turns. Answer: sometimes. Two small acute turns together can be acute. Two bigger acute turns together can make a right angle or an obtuse angle.
feedback: As the straw turns, the wedge grows and the read-out shows the turn in words. When the straw stops, the name card that fits lights up softly.
A name card that does not fit slides back with a clue, for example: The straw is less than the quarter-turn mark. Is that wider or narrower than a right angle?
With the guide on, the straw snaps lightly to the quarter-turn mark and the half-turn mark, and the tool says, for example: This is exactly a quarter turn: a right angle.
After Add a turn the tool shows the two turns joined as a sum, for example 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, and names the angle they make together.
On the fan the same wedge and names appear, and the tool counts how many different acute and obtuse angles have been shown.
tool_config.done_when: The five practice angles are made and named, the fan shows two acute and two obtuse angles, and the student has answered the question about two acute turns.

X is exactly a quarter turn: a right angle. 3. Y is less than a quarter turn: an acute angle. 4. Z is more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn: an obtuse angle. 5. Check: X, Y and Z were all compared with the same quarter turn. Answer: X: a right angle; Y: an acute angle; Z: an obtuse angle

media.context: Angles as Turns. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show that two quarter turns make a half turn, a straight angle, and that a turn of 3/4 is more than a straight angle. It works this example: Pragya's paper fan opens by a half turn and then by one more quarter turn in the same direction. What turn is that in all, and how does it compare with a straight angle?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Pragya turns the yellow straw a quarter turn, then another quarter turn the same way. What do the two straws look like now? Two quarter turns make a half turn: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. The two straws lie in one straight line. This angle is called a straight angle. A 3/4 turn is more than a half turn, so it is more than a straight angle. A full turn brings the straw back to where it started. The paper fan shows them all with one side fixed: a full turn, a 1/2 turn (a straight angle), a 1/4 turn (a right angle), less than a 1/4 turn (an acute angle), and between a 1/4 and a 1/2 turn (an obtuse angle). Rule: a 1/2 turn is a straight angle, and a 3/4 turn is more than a straight angle. 1. A half turn is 1/2 and a quarter turn is 1/4. 1/2 is the same as 2/4. 2. In all: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. 3. A straight angle is a 1/2 turn, which is 2/4. 3/4 is more than 2/4. 4. So the turn is 3/4, more than a straight angle. 5. Check: 3 quarter turns are one quarter turn short of a full turn. Answer: A 3/4 turn, more than a straight angle

content.question: Make an acute turn with the straws or fan. Continue to make another acute turn. Can the two acute turns together make another acute turn?
steps: An acute turn is less than a quarter turn.
Make two small acute turns, one after the other. Together they can still be less than a quarter turn: acute.
Make two bigger turns that are each almost a quarter turn. Together they are more than a quarter turn, so the angle can be obtuse.
Two acute turns can also add up to exactly a quarter turn: a right angle.
So it depends on how big each turn is.
content.answer: Sometimes. Two small acute turns together can be acute; two bigger ones can make a right angle or an obtuse angle.

content.text:
Let us make our tool to measure turns.
Cut out a circle from a tracing paper and fold it to make 8 equal parts.
Attach a straw to the centre and mark the starting point as shown.
Now, cut out 1/8 part and 2/8 parts of the circle and paste them on a thicker paper or board. Use these as angle measuring tools.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a circle is folded into 8 equal parts and a straw turns 2 parts from the starting point. What fraction of a full turn is that?
2. Cut a circle from tracing paper and fold it into 8 equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre and mark the starting point A.
3. Each part is 1/8 of a full turn. Turn the straw 1 part: a 1/8 turn. Turn it 2 parts: a 2/8 turn.
4. 2 parts are 2/8, the same as 1/4: a quarter turn, a right angle. A 1/8 turn is half of a quarter turn.
5. 4 parts are 4/8, the same as 1/2: a half turn, a straight angle. 6 parts are 6/8, the same as 3/4. 8 parts are 8/8, a full turn.
6. You can cut out the 1/8 part and the 2/8 part and paste them on a thicker paper or board to use as angle measuring tools.
7. Rule: n parts of the 8 make an n/8 turn. 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4 and 8/8 is a full turn.

content.text:
Worked example: The straw on the circle with 8 equal parts turns 5 parts, and then 2 more parts in the same direction. What turn is that, and how much more is needed for a full turn?
1. Each part is a 1/8 turn.
2. 5 parts and 2 more parts make 5 + 2 = 7 parts.
3. 7 parts of the 8 make a 7/8 turn.
4. A full turn is 8 parts, and 8 − 7 = 1.
5. So 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, completes the full turn.
6. Check: 5/8 + 2/8 = 7/8, and 7/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1.
Answer: A 7/8 turn; 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, makes a full turn

content.text:
Now, cut out a circle from a tracing paper. First, fold the circle in half, and then fold it again into 3 equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre of the circle. Mark the starting point.
Cut out 1/6 part and 2/6 part of the circle. Fold one of the 1/6 parts into half.
This is the same as a 1/12 turn.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a circle is folded into 6 equal parts. What fraction of a full turn is each part? And if one part is folded in half, what fraction is each small part?
2. Fold a circle in half, then fold each half into 3 equal parts. Now it has 2 × 3 = 6 equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre and mark the starting point.
3. Each part is a 1/6 turn. Turn the straw 1/6, 2/6, and so on until the full circle: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, and 6/6 is a full turn.
4. Cut out the 1/6 part and the 2/6 part. Fold one 1/6 part in half. Each half of a 1/6 part is a 1/12 turn.
5. Rule: the circle in 6 parts gives 1/6 turns. Half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn, and 12 of them make a full turn.

content.text:
Worked example: How many 1/12 pieces cover a 1/6 piece, a 2/6 piece and a 3/6 piece?
1. A 1/12 piece is half of a 1/6 piece, so 2 pieces of 1/12 cover a 1/6 piece.
2. A 2/6 piece is 2 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 2 × 2 = 4 pieces of 1/12.
3. A 3/6 piece is 3 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 3 × 2 = 6 pieces of 1/12.
4. Check: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, and 6 pieces of 1/12 make 6/12 = 1/2.
Answer: 2 pieces, 4 pieces and 6 pieces of 1/12

media.title: Turn Disc

tool_config.title: Turn Disc
tool_config.idea: Measure turns on a disc cut into equal parts, one division at a time: Stage 1 eighths, Stage 2 sixths, Stage 3 twelfths. A turn is always told as a part of a full turn. A stage opens only after the one before is done, and the divisions are never mixed on one disc.
tool_config.screen: A craft table in the classroom, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. In the middle, large, lies the tracing-paper disc with fold lines, a straw fixed at its centre and the starting point A marked on the edge, as in your maths book. A teal start mark sits at A and never moves; an orange curved arrow and a shaded wedge grow from A as the straw turns. Three stage tabs sit at the top, Stage 1: Eighths, Stage 2: Sixths and Stage 3: Twelfths; a stage opens when the one before is done, and each stage shows its own disc: 8 equal parts, 6 equal parts or 12 equal parts. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the straw round (it snaps to the fold lines) or press the plus and minus buttons to move it one part at a time; a Show equal names button that writes the equal fractions for the turn (for example 2/8 = 1/4); in Stage 3, a place to drag the 1/12 pieces onto a 1/6 piece; Check, Hint, Retry (puts the straw back on A), Reset (restores the stage), Back and Next in the same places on every card. media.description: Concept video: Show how a circle folded into 8 equal parts measures turns in eighths, with 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4 and 8/8 a full turn. It works this example: The straw on the circle with 8 equal parts turns 5 parts, and then 2 more parts in the same direction. What turn is that, and how much more is needed for a full turn?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a circle is folded into 8 equal parts and a straw turns 2 parts from the starting point. What fraction of a full turn is that? Cut a circle from tracing paper and fold it into 8 equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre and mark the starting point A. Each part is 1/8 of a full turn. Turn the straw 1 part: a 1/8 turn. Turn it 2 parts: a 2/8 turn. 2 parts are 2/8, the same as 1/4: a quarter turn, a right angle. A 1/8 turn is half of a quarter turn. 4 parts are 4/8, the same as 1/2: a half turn, a straight angle. 6 parts are 6/8, the same as 3/4. 8 parts are 8/8, a full turn. You can cut out the 1/8 part and the 2/8 part and paste them on a thicker paper or board to use as angle measuring tools. Rule: n parts of the 8 make an n/8 turn. 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4 and 8/8 is a full turn. 1. Each part is a 1/8 turn. 2. 5 parts and 2 more parts make 5 + 2 = 7 parts. 3. 7 parts of the 8 make a 7/8 turn. 4. A full turn is 8 parts, and 8 − 7 = 1. 5. So 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, completes the full turn. 6. Check: 5/8 + 2/8 = 7/8, and 7/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1. Answer: A 7/8 turn; 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, makes a full turn

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a circle is folded into 6 equal parts. What fraction of a full turn is each part? And if one part is folded in half, what fraction is each small part? Fold a circle in half, then fold each half into 3 equal parts. Now it has 2 × 3 = 6 equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre and mark the starting point. Each part is a 1/6 turn. Turn the straw 1/6, 2/6, and so on until the full circle: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, and 6/6 is a full turn. Cut out the 1/6 part and the 2/6 part. Fold one 1/6 part in half. Each half of a 1/6 part is a 1/12 turn. Rule: the circle in 6 parts gives 1/6 turns. Half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn, and 12 of them make a full turn. 1. A 1/12 piece is half of a 1/6 piece, so 2 pieces of 1/12 cover a 1/6 piece. 2. A 2/6 piece is 2 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 2 × 2 = 4 pieces of 1/12. 3. A 3/6 piece is 3 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 3 × 2 = 6 pieces of 1/12. 4. Check: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, and 6 pieces of 1/12 make 6/12 = 1/2. Answer: 2 pieces, 4 pieces and 6 pieces of 1/12

steps: The circle is folded into 8 equal parts. Each part is a 1/8 turn.
A 1/8 turn is 1 part from the starting point A.
A 2/8 turn is 2 parts from A.
A 1/4 turn is the same as 2/8, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2 parts. So it is also 2 parts from A.
A 3/8 turn is 3 parts from A.

content.answer: 1/8: 1 part; 2/8: 2 parts; 1/4: 2 parts, the same as 2/8; 3/8: 3 parts.

2. $\frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}$, because $4 \div 4 = 1$ and $8 \div 4 = 2$.

4. Check: $\frac{4}{8} = \frac{2}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$, which is two quarter turns.
Answer: A straight angle, because $\frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}$ is a half turn.

content.question: Show the turns of the straw equal to 1/6, 2/6, and so on until you complete a full circle.
steps: The circle is folded in half, then each half into 3 equal parts: 2 × 3 = 6 equal parts.
Each part is a 1/6 turn.
Turn the straw 1 part at a time from the starting point: 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, 6/6.
2/6 = 1/3 and 3/6 = 1/2, a half turn, a straight angle. 4/6 = 2/3.
At 6/6 the straw is back on the starting point: a full turn.
Check: 6 parts of 1/6 make 6/6 = 1.
content.answer: The straw turns 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6 and 6/6; 6/6 is a full turn.

content.question: Can you guess what turn of the straw will be equal to half of a 1/6 turn?
steps: A 1/6 part is folded in half, so it is cut into 2 equal small parts.
The whole circle has 6 parts of 1/6, and each is cut into 2 small parts: 6 × 2 = 12 small parts.
So each small part is 1 of 12 equal parts: a 1/12 turn.
Check: 2 small parts make 2/12 = 1/6.
content.answer: A 1/12 turn.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an angle is just covered by a 1/6 piece and a 1/12 piece side by side. How much of a full turn is the angle?
2. Your angle measuring tools are pieces of a circle: 1/8, 2/8, 1/6, 2/6 and 1/12. Lay the pieces side by side, starting on the first line of the angle.
3. Guess first, then check. You may need a combination of pieces.
4. Add the fractions of the pieces. To add 1/6 and 1/12, use twelfths: a 1/6 piece is 2 pieces of 1/12.
5. Then name the angle: less than 1/4 turn is acute, exactly 1/4 is right, and between 1/4 and 1/2 is obtuse.
6. Rule: lay the pieces side by side from the first line, add their turns, and compare the total with 1/4 and 1/2.

content.text:
Worked example: An angle is covered exactly by one 1/6 piece and one 1/12 piece laid side by side. What turn does the angle make, and what kind of angle is it?
1. Lay the 1/6 piece on the angle, starting from the first line, and the 1/12 piece next to it.
2. 1/6 is 2 pieces of 1/12, so 1/6 = 2/12.
3. 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12.
4. 3/12 = 1/4, because 3 ÷ 3 = 1 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
5. A 1/4 turn is a right angle.
6. Check: 3 pieces of 1/12 make a quarter turn, and 12 pieces make a full turn.
Answer: A 1/4 turn: a right angle

content.question: Guess the measures of each of the angles shown below. Then, check using your angle measuring tools. You may need to use a combination of measures. Also, state whether each of the angles is acute, right, or obtuse.
steps: The pieces are 1/8, 2/8 (a 1/4), 1/6, 2/6 (a 1/3) and 1/12. Lay them side by side on each angle.
Angle 1: the narrowest, about one 1/12 piece: about a 1/12 turn. It is less than 1/4, so acute.
Angle 2: one 1/6 piece: a 1/6 turn. Acute.
Angle 3: one 1/8 piece: a 1/8 turn. Acute.
Angle 4: about one 1/6 piece: about a 1/6 turn. Acute.
Angle 5: one 2/8 piece: 2/8 = 1/4, a right angle.
Angle 6: about one 2/6 piece: about 2/6 = 1/3, more than 1/4 and less than 1/2, so obtuse.
Angle 7: a 1/8 piece and a 2/8 piece: 1/8 + 2/8 = 3/8, more than 1/4 and less than 1/2, so obtuse.
Check: 1/12, 1/6, 1/8 and 1/6 are each less than 1/4, so those four are acute.
content.answer: 1: about 1/12, acute; 2: 1/6, acute; 3: 1/8, acute; 4: about 1/6, acute; 5: 1/4, right; 6: about 1/3, obtuse; 7: 3/8, obtuse.
content.text:
1. The pieces are $\frac{1}{8}$, $\frac{2}{8} (a \frac{1}{4})$, $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{2}{6} (a \frac{1}{3})$ and $\frac{1}{12}$. Lay them side by side on each angle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have a line and you need an angle of a 1/2 + 1/12 turn. How can you draw it?
2. Put one end of the line at the centre of the circle pieces. This end is the corner of the angle.
3. Lay the pieces for the turn one after another, starting from the line. For 1/2 + 1/12, lay a half turn, then a 1/12 piece.
4. Draw the second line along the edge of the last piece.
5. A 1/4 turn gives a right angle, a 1/2 turn gives a straight angle, and a turn of more than 1/2 is more than a straight angle.
6. Rule: lay the pieces of the turn from the given line and draw along the last edge.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw an angle of a 1/2 + 1/12 turn on a given line. What kind of angle is it?
1. Turn the line a half turn, then 1/12 more, in the same direction.
2. 1/2 = 6/12, so 1/2 + 1/12 = 6/12 + 1/12 = 7/12.
3. A half turn is 6/12, and 7/12 is more than 6/12.
4. So the angle is more than a half turn: more than a straight angle.
5. Draw the second line along the edge of the 1/12 piece.
6. Check: 7 pieces of 1/12 are one piece more than the half turn of 6 pieces.
Answer: A 7/12 turn, more than a straight angle

tool_config.idea: One purpose, the size of an angle as a turn, in two clearly separated activities. Activity 1, Measure (first): guess the turn an angle makes and check it by laying the turn pieces side by side on it, name the angle as acute, right or obtuse, and read the turn an arrow makes. Activity 2, Draw (second): draw a second line to make an angle for a given turn. Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done.
tool_config.screen: A craft table with dotted paper, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Two big activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: Measure and Activity 2: Draw; only one activity is on screen at a time, and Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done. In the middle, large, is a sheet of dotted paper. In Activity 1 an angle is drawn on it from a dot, two lines meeting at the corner. In Activity 2 a given line with a dot at each end is drawn on it. At the side lies a tray of five wedge pieces cut from the tracing-paper circle, each with its fraction written on it: 1/8, 2/8 (also marked 1/4), 1/6, 2/6 (also marked 1/3) and 1/12, which are the angle measuring tools of your maths book. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls in Activity 1: a guess box with number buttons to type a guess such as 1/6; drag a wedge piece into the angle (it snaps with its point at the corner and its first edge on the first line; the next piece snaps after it); tap a piece to take it back; three name cards, acute, right and obtuse, to tap. Controls in Activity 2: plus and minus buttons that turn a second line by one piece at a time from the given line, and a Draw button that fixes the line. In both: Check, Hint, Retry (clears the pieces or the line on this card), Reset (restores the activity), Undo, Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the pieces laid so far as a sum, for example 1/6 + 1/12; the total as a fraction of a full turn, for example 3/12 = 1/4; in Activity 1 the angle name once it fits; and a card number, Activity 1 cards 1 to 4 and Activity 2 cards 1 to 3.
student_does: Activity 1: look at the angle covered by a 1/6 piece and a 1/12 piece from the video. Guess how much of a full turn it is, then lay the pieces on it to check.
Activity 1 (Measure): guess and check two practice angles and read the turn an arrow makes between two arrows. Activity 2 (Draw): draw second lines for a 1/6 turn and for a 1/2 + 1/12 turn.
Activity 1: guess and check the book's seven angles and say whether each is acute, right or obtuse. Activity 2: draw the book's angles for the given turns using the given lines.
challenges: Activity 1, card 1 (practice values): an angle is covered by a 1/4 piece and a 1/12 piece. Guess, then check. What turn is it, and what kind of angle? Answer: 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3, more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: obtuse.
Activity 1, card 2 (practice values): an angle is covered by two 1/8 pieces. What turn is it, and what kind of angle? Answer: 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4: a right angle.

Activity 1, card 3 (practice values): an arrow turns from straight up, through straight down, and then a 1/6 piece more, in the same direction. What turn has it made? Answer: 1/2 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6, more than a half turn.

Activity 1, card 4: 'Guess the measures of each of the angles shown below. Then, check using your angle measuring tools. You may need to use a combination of measures. Also, state whether each of the angles is acute, right, or obtuse.' Use the seven angles of your maths book. Answer: about 1/12, 1/6, 1/8, about 1/6, 1/4, about 1/3 and 3/8, named acute, acute, acute, acute, right, obtuse and obtuse.
Activity 2, card 1: draw a second line on the given line so that the angle is a 1/6 turn. Answer: one 1/6 piece from the given line. It is less than a 1/4, so it is acute.
Activity 2, card 2 (practice values): draw a second line so that the angle is a 1/2 + 1/12 turn. Answer: 1/2 + 1/12 = 6/12 + 1/12 = 7/12, more than a half turn, so more than a straight angle.

Activity 2, card 3: 'Draw angles for the given measures of turns using the given lines.' Use the five lines of your maths book, each with the turn written beside it: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12 and 1/4. Answer: 1/2 gives a straight line, each 1/4 gives a square corner, 1/8 gives half a square corner and 1/12 a narrower angle. Either end of the line can be the corner.
feedback: Activity 1: laying a piece shows the sum so far, for example 1/6 + 1/12, and the total as a fraction of a full turn. When the pieces fill the angle exactly the tool says: The pieces fit.
Activity 1: if the pieces are too few or too many a soft amber note says so, for example: There is a gap of one 1/12 piece, or: The pieces go past the second line.
Activity 1: the total is compared with 1/4 and 1/2 and the angle is named, for example: 4/12 is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: obtuse.
Activity 2: the second line turns piece by piece and the shaded wedge grows; Draw fixes it and the tool checks the total against the turn asked.
A guess that is close is accepted with the note: Your guess is near. The pieces say it is exactly 1/6.

content.question: Draw angles for the given measures of turns using the given lines.
steps: Take one end of each line as the corner of the angle. Turn the line by the given part of a full turn and draw the second line.

steps: Draw each angle from a line. Turn the line the given part of a full turn.
1/2 turn: a straight angle.
1/4 turn: a right angle.
2/4 turn: 2/4 = 1/2, so it is a straight angle.
1/6 turn: less than a 1/4 turn, so it is an acute angle.
4/6 turn: 4/6 is more than 3/6, and 3/6 is 1/2. So it is more than a straight angle.
3/12 turn: 3/12 = 1/4, a right angle.
1/2 + 1/4 turn: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4, more than 1/2: more than a straight angle.

1/8 + 1/6 turn: 1/6 is more than 1/8, so the total is more than 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4. Each part is less than 1/4, so the total is less than 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. It is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: an obtuse angle.
Check: 2/4 and 1/2 are the same turn, and 3/12 and 1/4 are the same turn.
content.answer: 1/2 and 2/4: straight; 1/4 and 3/12: right; 1/6: acute; 4/6 and 1/2 + 1/4: more than straight; 1/8 + 1/6: obtuse.

concepts.concept_name: Minutes and Turns of the Minute Hand

content.text:
1. Predict first: the minute hand moves for 15 minutes. What part of a full turn has it made?
2. The minute hand makes a full turn in 60 minutes. It comes back to where it started.
3. A 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. So going from one number of the clock to the next is a 1/12 turn.
4. 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn, because 15 × 4 = 60. 30 minutes is a 1/2 turn, 45 minutes is a 3/4 turn and 60 minutes is a full turn.
5. The hand turns from where it starts, not always from 12. To find where it stops, move it the minutes the way a clock moves from its starting place.
6. Rule: 60 minutes is a full turn, 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, and the hand turns from where it starts.

content.text:
Worked example: The minute hand starts at the number 2 and moves 25 minutes. What turn does it make, and where does it stop?
1. The hand starts at 2, which is the 10 minute mark, because 2 × 5 = 10.
2. A 1/12 turn is 5 minutes. 25 minutes is 25 ÷ 5 = 5 of these.
3. So the turn is 5/12 of a full turn.
4. The hand stops at the 10 + 25 = 35 minute mark.
5. 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the hand stops at the number 7.
6. Check: from 2 to 7 is 5 numbers, and each step from one number to the next is a 1/12 turn, so the turn is 5/12.
Answer: A 5/12 turn; the hand stops at 7

tool_config.title: Minute Hand Turner
tool_config.idea: Link the minutes the minute hand moves to the fraction of a full turn it makes: 60 minutes is a full turn, so 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn, 30 is a 1/2 turn, 45 is a 3/4 turn and 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, and the hand turns from the place where it starts.
tool_config.screen: The clock on the school wall, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The clock face is large and fills the middle of the screen, with the numbers 1 to 12 and a ring of minute marks, and a long minute hand. A teal dot marks the starting place of the hand; an orange shaded sweep grows from the start as the hand turns, and a curved arrow follows the hand in the way a clock moves. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the minute hand the way a clock moves (it snaps to the 5 minute marks, and a Show single minutes switch adds the minute marks between); plus 5 and minus 5 minute buttons; a Start at selector that places the starting dot at any number of the clock; fraction cards, 1/12, 1/6, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 and 3/4, to tap so that the hand turns that part; answer boxes for the turn and for the minutes; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the hand to its starting place), Reset (restores the clock), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: moved by a number of minutes; turn as a fraction of a full turn; the number the hand points at now; and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the minute hand turning from 12 round to 3 in the video. Drag it and watch the minutes. How many minutes is a full turn of the minute hand?
Move the hand by minutes from different starting places and read the turn, give the hand a fraction card and read the minutes, and find where the hand stops.

The book's questions about the minute hand: the turn after 15, 30 and 45 minutes, and the minutes after turns of 1/12, a full circle, 1/6 and 4/12, with the starting place of the hand given each time.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): start at 12 and move the hand 20 minutes. What turn is it, and where does the hand stop? Answer: 20 × 3 = 60, so it is a 1/3 turn. The hand stops at 4.
Card 2 (practice values): start at 6 and move the hand 5 minutes. What turn is it? Answer: 60 ÷ 12 = 5, so 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn. The hand stops at 7.

Card 3 (practice values): start at 2 and move the hand 25 minutes. What turn is it, and where does the hand stop? Answer: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 pieces of 1/12, so it is a 5/12 turn. The hand starts at the 10 minute mark and stops at the 35 minute mark, the number 7.
Card 4: tap the fraction card 1/2. How many minutes does the hand move? Answer: 30 minutes, because 30 × 2 = 60.

Card 5 (practice values): start at 8 and move the hand 40 minutes. What turn is it, and where does the hand stop? Answer: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 pieces of 1/12, so it is an 8/12 turn. The hand starts at the 40 minute mark and stops at the 20 minute mark, the number 4.

Challenge: 'Guess the measure of turns the minute hand of a clock makes in each of the following cases. The initial position of the minute hand is given. Draw the final position of the minute hand on the clock face. Discuss your reasoning in class. (a) When the minute hand moves by 15 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (b) When the minute hand moves by 30 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (c) When the minute hand moves by 45 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle.' The hand starts at 3 in (a), at 6 in (b) and at 9 in (c). Answer: (a) 1/4 turn, the hand stops at 6; (b) 1/2 turn, it stops at 12; (c) 3/4 turn, it stops at 6.

Challenge: '(d) When the minute hand has turned by 1/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (e) When the minute hand has turned a full-circle, it has moved by ___ minutes. (f) When the minute hand has turned by 1/6 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (g) When the minute hand has turned by 4/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes.' The hand starts at 1 in (d), at 12 in (e), at 2 in (f) and at 4 in (g). Answer: (d) 5 minutes, it stops at 2; (e) 60 minutes, it stops at 12; (f) 10 minutes, it stops at 4; (g) 20 minutes, it stops at 8.
feedback: As the hand moves, the sweep grows and the read-outs show the minutes moved and the turn as a fraction of a full turn, for example 15 minutes, a 1/4 turn.
A wrong turn shows a soft amber note, for example: A full turn is 60 minutes. 15 minutes is 15 × 4 = 60, so it is a 1/4 turn.
The hand always turns from the starting dot, not from 12, and the tool says so, for example: The hand started at 2, so it stops at 7, not at 5.
A fraction card turns the hand that part of a full turn and shows the minutes, for example: 1/12 of 60 minutes is 5 minutes.
When the hand is back on the starting dot the note says: a full turn, 60 minutes.
tool_config.done_when: The five practice cards are done with the turn and the stopping place read correctly, and the student has answered all seven parts of the book's minute hand question.

Tap plus 5 until the read-out shows the minutes for this card, read the turn, and see which number the hand points at.

media.description: Concept video: Show that a full turn of the minute hand is 60 minutes, so 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, 15 minutes a 1/4 turn and so on, and how to find where the hand stops from where it starts. It works this example: The minute hand starts at the number 2 and moves 25 minutes. What turn does it make, and where does it stop?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: the minute hand moves for 15 minutes. What part of a full turn has it made? The minute hand makes a full turn in 60 minutes. It comes back to where it started. A 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. So going from one number of the clock to the next is a 1/12 turn. 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn, because 15 × 4 = 60. 30 minutes is a 1/2 turn, 45 minutes is a 3/4 turn and 60 minutes is a full turn. The hand turns from where it starts, not always from 12. To find where it stops, move it the minutes the way a clock moves from its starting place. Rule: 60 minutes is a full turn, 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, and the hand turns from where it starts. 1. The hand starts at 2, which is the 10 minute mark, because 2 × 5 = 10. 2. A 1/12 turn is 5 minutes. 25 minutes is 25 ÷ 5 = 5 of these. 3. So the turn is 5/12 of a full turn. 4. The hand stops at the 10 + 25 = 35 minute mark. 5. 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the hand stops at the number 7. 6. Check: from 2 to 7 is 5 numbers, and each step from one number to the next is a 1/12 turn, so the turn is 5/12. Answer: A 5/12 turn; the hand stops at 7

content.question: Guess the measure of turns the minute hand of a clock makes in each of the following cases. The initial position of the minute hand is given. Draw the final position of the minute hand on the clock face. Discuss your reasoning in class. (a): When the minute hand moves by 15 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (b): When the minute hand moves by 30 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (c): When the minute hand moves by 45 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (d): When the minute hand has turned by 1/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (e): When the minute hand has turned a full-circle, it has moved by ___ minutes. (f): When the minute hand has turned by 1/6 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (g): When the minute hand has turned by 4/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes.
steps: A full turn of the minute hand is 60 minutes. A 1/12 turn is 5 minutes.
(a): 15 minutes: 15 × 4 = 60, so it is a 1/4 turn. The hand starts at 3 and stops at 6.
(b): 30 minutes: 30 × 2 = 60, so it is a 1/2 turn. From 6 the hand stops at 12.
(c): 45 minutes: 3 × 15 = 45, so it is 3 quarter turns, a 3/4 turn. From 9 the hand stops at 6.
(d): a 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. From 1 the hand stops at 2.
(e): a full circle is 60 minutes. The hand starts and stops at 12.
(f): a 1/6 turn is 60 ÷ 6 = 10 minutes. From 2 the hand stops at 4.
(g): a 4/12 turn is 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, because one 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. From 4 the hand stops at 8.
Check: 4/12 is the same as 1/3, and 20 × 3 = 60.
content.text:
1. A full turn of the minute hand is $60$ minutes. A $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $5$ minutes.
2. $(a)$: $15$ minutes: $15 \times 4 = 60$, so it is a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn. The hand starts at $3$ and stops at $6$.
3. $(b)$: $30$ minutes: $30 \times 2 = 60$, so it is a $\frac{1}{2}$ turn. From $6$ the hand stops at $12$.
4. $(c)$: $45$ minutes: $3 \times 15 = 45$, so it is $3$ quarter turns, a $\frac{3}{4}$ turn. From $9$ the hand stops at $6$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
5. $(d)$: a $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $60 \div 12 = 5$ minutes. From $1$ the hand stops at $2$.
6. $(e)$: a full circle is $60$ minutes. The hand starts and stops at $12$.
7. $(f)$: a $\frac{1}{6}$ turn is $60 \div 6 = 10$ minutes. From $2$ the hand stops at $4$.
8. $(g)$: a $\frac{4}{12}$ turn is $4 \times 5 = 20$ minutes, because one $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $60 \div 12 = 5$ minutes. From $4$ the hand stops at $8$.
9. Check: $\frac{4}{12}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{3}$, and $20 \times 3 = 60$.
Answer: $(a)$: $\frac{1}{4}$; $(b)$: $\frac{1}{2}$; $(c)$: $\frac{3}{4}$; $(d)$: $5$; $(e)$: $60$; $(f)$: $10$; $(g)$: $20$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

(d): a 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. From 1 the hand stops at 2. 6. (e): a full circle is 60 minutes. The hand starts and stops at 12. 7. (f): a 1/6 turn is 60 ÷ 6 = 10 minutes. From 2 the hand stops at 4. 8. (g): a 4/12 turn is 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, because one 1/12 turn is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes. From 4 the hand stops at 8. 9. Check: 4/12 is the same as 1/3, and 20 × 3 = 60. Answer: (a): 1/4; (b): 1/2; (c): 3/4; (d): 5; (e): 60; (f): 10; (g): 20.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an arrow points down and makes a quarter turn to point left. Is it turning the way the hands of a clock move?
2. The hands of a clock move round from 12 to 1 to 2 and on. The direction in which the hands of a clock move is called clockwise movement.
3. The opposite movement is called anti-clockwise movement.
4. Find the turn on the clock face. From 6 to 9 is the way a clock moves, so it is clockwise. From 9 to 6 is the other way, so it is anti-clockwise.
5. Rule: with the hands of a clock is clockwise, and against them is anti-clockwise.

content.text:
Worked example: An arrow points down. It makes a quarter turn and now points left. Is the turn clockwise or anti-clockwise?
1. Think of the arrow as a clock hand pointing at 6, straight down.
2. Left is the 9 on a clock.
3. A clock hand goes from 6 to 7, 8 and 9. That is the way a clock moves.
4. So the turn is clockwise.
5. Check: the other way from 6 is 5, 4 and 3, which points right, not left.
Answer: Clockwise

concepts.concept_name: Finding the Final Direction After Right-Angle Turns

content.text:
1. Predict first: you face West and turn 3 right angles anti-clockwise. Which direction do you face?
2. The four directions are North at the top, East on the right, South at the bottom and West on the left. A right angle is a quarter turn.
3. Recap: clockwise goes North, East, South, West, North, and so on. Anti-clockwise goes the other way: North, West, South, East, North.
4. Count the right angles one by one. Two right angles are a half turn. Four right angles are a full turn and bring you back to where you started.
5. A half turn ends in the same place either way, but a quarter turn does not.
6. A 1/2 right angle is half of a right angle. Two of them make 1 right angle.
7. Rule: count the right angles in the turn, move that many directions clockwise or anti-clockwise, and four right angles bring you back.

content.text:
Worked example: Padma faces West and turns 3 right angles anti-clockwise. Which direction does she face?
1. Anti-clockwise from West, the order is West, South, East, North.
2. 1 right angle anti-clockwise: South.
3. 2 right angles: East.
4. 3 right angles: North.
5. So she faces North.
6. Check: 3 right angles anti-clockwise is the same as 1 right angle clockwise, because 3 + 1 = 4. West turned 1 right angle clockwise is North.
Answer: North

tool_config.title: Turn and Face
tool_config.idea: Find the direction faced after turns of right angles. Activity 1 is a short recap of clockwise and anti-clockwise: clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move and anti-clockwise is the other way. Activity 2 is the main work: turn a child on a compass by right angles from a starting direction and read the final direction faced.
tool_config.screen: A compass painted on the playground ground, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The compass is large in the middle, with North at the top, East on the right, South at the bottom and West on the left, each named on a signboard, and a child stands at the centre and turns on the spot. A small clock sits in the corner with its hand moving the way a clock moves, to show clockwise. Two activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: Which way? (a short recap) and Activity 2: Where do I face?; only one is on screen at a time, and Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: two big buttons, Clockwise and Anti-clockwise, that pick the direction; turn buttons, 1 right angle and 1/2 right angle, that turn the child that much in the picked direction each time they are tapped; Undo, which takes back the last turn; a Start facing selector for North, East, South and West; answer boxes for the ending direction; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the child to the starting direction), Reset (restores the tool), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the turns made so far as a sum of right angles, for example 2 right angles clockwise; the direction faced now; and a card number, Activity 1 card 1 and Activity 2 cards 1 to 6.
student_does: Activity 1, a short recap: look at the arrow turning the way a clock moves. Press Clockwise and watch the child turn one right angle, then press Anti-clockwise and watch the child turn the other way.
Activity 2: turn the child by right angles from different starting directions, clockwise and anti-clockwise, and read the direction faced at the end.
Activity 2: complete the table of directions after turns, and find the place Padma faces after a half turn clockwise and another way to turn to face it.
challenges: Activity 1, recap, card 1: start facing North. Press Clockwise and turn 1 right angle, then undo, press Anti-clockwise and turn 1 right angle. Which way did the child go each time, and where does each end? Answer: clockwise went the way a clock moves, from North to East; anti-clockwise went the other way, from North to West.
Activity 2, card 1 (practice values): start facing East. Press Clockwise and turn 1 right angle. Which direction do you face? Answer: South. The clockwise order is North, East, South, West.

Activity 2, card 2 (practice values): start facing West. Press Anti-clockwise and turn 3 right angles. Which direction do you face? Answer: North. Anti-clockwise from West the order is South, East, North.

Activity 2, card 3: start facing North and turn a half turn, 2 right angles, clockwise. Then undo and turn a half turn anti-clockwise. Where does each end? Answer: both end facing South. A half turn ends in the same place either way.

Activity 2, card 4: start facing North and turn 1 right angle clockwise, then undo and turn 1 right angle anti-clockwise. Where does each end? Answer: East and West. A quarter turn ends in different places.

Activity 2, card 5: 'The children in a class are playing a game in which the teacher tells them the direction in which they should rotate. Complete the table by filling the direction the children will face on completing the given turns. The starting direction is given in the table.' The seven rows of your maths book are used. Answer: South, North, East, West, East, South, and for the last row the number is not printed, so the rule is shown (if it is 3, North).

Activity 2, card 6: 'Padma is facing the toy shop. What place will she face if she takes a half turn clockwise? What other way can she turn to face the same place?' Answer: Padma faces the ice cream cart, and she can also take a half turn anti-clockwise.
feedback: Each tap turns the child and adds to the sum, for example 2 right angles clockwise, and the direction faced now is shown on the compass.
A wrong ending direction shows a soft amber note, for example: From North, clockwise: East, South. 2 right angles end at South.
Turns of 4 right angles are shown as a full turn with the note: back where you started. 5 right angles are shown as 4 right angles and 1 more.
Half a right angle turns the child half way between two directions, and two of them together make 1 right angle.

Check: 3 right angles anti-clockwise is the same as 1 right angle clockwise, because 3 + 1 = 4. West turned 1 right angle clockwise is North. Answer: North

content.question: The children in a class are playing a game in which the teacher tells them the direction in which they should rotate. Complete the table by filling the direction the children will face on completing the given turns. The starting direction is given in the table. (a): North, two right angles clockwise; (b): South, two right angles anti-clockwise; (c): East, four right angles anti-clockwise; (d): West, four right angles clockwise; (e): North, 5 right angles clockwise; (f): South, 3 right angles clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise; (g): West, ___ right angles clockwise, four 1/2 right angles anti-clockwise
steps: The directions go clockwise: North, East, South, West. A right angle is a quarter turn, one step.
(a): North, 2 right angles clockwise: East, then South. It ends at South.
(b): South, 2 right angles anti-clockwise: East, then North. It ends at North.
(c): East, 4 right angles anti-clockwise: a full turn, back at East.
(d): West, 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at West.
(e): North, 5 right angles clockwise: 4 of them are a full turn, and 5 − 4 = 1 more takes it to East.
(f): South, 3 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at South.

(g): West. Four 1/2 right angles are 2 right angles anti-clockwise. The number before 'right angles clockwise' is not printed in your maths book. The end is West turned that number minus 2 right angles clockwise. Sample: if it is 3, then 3 − 2 = 1 right angle clockwise, and West ends at North.
Check: (c), (d) and (f) are full turns, so they end where they started.
content.answer: (a): South; (b): North; (c): East; (d): West; (e): East; (f): South; (g): the number is not printed; if it is 3, North.

media.teaching_notes: 1. The directions go clockwise: North, East, South, West. A right angle is a quarter turn, one step. 2. (a): North, 2 right angles clockwise: East, then South. It ends at South. 3. (b): South, 2 right angles anti-clockwise: East, then North. It ends at North. 4. (c): East, 4 right angles anti-clockwise: a full turn, back at East. 5. (d): West, 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at West. 6. (e): North, 5 right angles clockwise: 4 of them are a full turn, and 5 − 4 = 1 more takes it to East. 7. (f): South, 3 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at South. 8. (g): West. Four 1/2 right angles are 2 right angles anti-clockwise. The number before 'right angles clockwise' is not printed in your maths book. The end is West turned that number minus 2 right angles clockwise. Sample: if it is 3, then 3 − 2 = 1 right angle clockwise, and West ends at North. 9. Check: (c), (d) and (f) are full turns, so they end where they started. Answer: (a): South; (b): North; (c): East; (d): West; (e): East; (f): South; (g): the number is not printed; if it is 3, North.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked all round the playground of turns. Can you say one idea from each stop? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Full turn and half turn: a full turn brings you back to the starting position, and a half turn leaves you facing the opposite way.
3. Check: Sahana turns until her back is to the door. Is it a full turn or a half turn? A half turn.
4. Halves and quarters: 2 half turns make a full turn, 2 quarter turns make a half turn, and 4 quarter turns make a full turn.
5. Check: 1 half turn and 2 quarter turns make 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, a full turn.
6. Everyday objects turn only so far. Compare the greatest turn with a quarter turn: less, equal or more.
7. Angles arise from turns: a 1/4 turn is a right angle, less than a 1/4 turn is an acute angle, more than a 1/4 turn and less than a 1/2 turn is an obtuse angle, and a 1/2 turn is a straight angle. A 3/4 turn is more than a straight angle.
8. Check: a turn of 1/3 is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2. Which kind of angle is it? An obtuse angle.
9. Measuring turns: a circle in 8 parts gives 1/8 turns, with 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2 and 6/8 = 3/4. A circle in 6 parts gives 1/6 turns, and half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn.
10. Check: how many 1/8 pieces make a quarter turn? 2 pieces, because 2/8 = 1/4.
11. Measuring angles: lay the pieces side by side and add their turns. 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, a right angle.
12. The minute hand makes a full turn in 60 minutes, so 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn and 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn.
13. Check: the minute hand moves 20 minutes. What turn is that? 20 × 3 = 60, so it is a 1/3 turn.
14. Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move. The opposite is anti-clockwise.
15. Check: you face East and turn 2 right angles clockwise. Which direction do you face? East, then South, then West: you face West.

objectives.objective_text: Students name a turn as a full turn or a half turn by comparing where something faces with where it faced at the start.
Students name which child in the statue game made a full turn and which made a half turn, and explain the answer by comparing each child with the start.
Students find the turn made when half turns and quarter turns are joined in the same direction.
Students find the turn made when half turns and quarter turns are joined in the same direction on the giant wheel.
Students compare the greatest turn of an object with a quarter turn and say whether it is less than, equal to or more than a quarter turn.
Students join half turns and quarter turns on the wheel, and tick whether the greatest turn of an object is less than, equal to or more than a 1/4 turn.
Students name a turn from a fixed straw as a right, acute or obtuse angle by comparing it with a quarter turn.
Students name a half turn as a straight angle and a turn of 3/4 as more than a straight angle.
Students show acute and obtuse angles with a turning fan, and name right, acute, obtuse and straight angles in pictures.
Students show a turn on a circle folded into 8 equal parts and read it as a fraction of a full turn, such as 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2.
Students show 1/6 and 2/6 turns on a circle folded into 6 equal parts and show that half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn.
Students show and read turns of 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8, 6/8 and 8/8, of sixths and of 1/12 on a disc, and find the starting arrow of a given turn.
Students measure an angle by laying turn pieces side by side on it and adding their fractions, and name the angle as acute, right or obtuse.
Students guess and check angles with turn pieces and read the turn an arrow makes.
Students draw an angle for a given turn by laying the pieces for that turn from a given line and drawing the second line along the last piece.
Students measure angles with turn pieces and then draw angles for given turns using the given lines.
Students find the turn the minute hand makes from the minutes it moves, find the minutes from the turn, and say where the hand stops.
Students find the turn or the minutes for each movement of the minute hand and mark where the hand stops.
Students tell whether a turn is clockwise or anti-clockwise by comparing it with the way the hands of a clock move.
Students find the direction faced after turns of right angles, clockwise or anti-clockwise, from North, East, South or West.
Students tick the direction of a quarter turn, fill in the ending direction after turns of right angles, and find the place faced after a half turn.
